Haenertsburg

By: Annalise Lubbe | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
From the highest coffee farm in the land, to rare birds and the tallest tree in the world, Haenertsburg in Magoebaskloof is a village shrouded in mist and a history dating back to the gold rush.

Unique Selling Point:
Haenertsburg is a little village on the slopes of the Wolkberg mountains in Magoebaskloof near Tzaneen in Limpopo. Rising 1,550 meters above sea level, the town is often shrouded in mist and clouds giving it the apt name of “Land of the Silver Mist”. The steepest mountain pass in South Africa, the Magoebaskloof pass (falling approximately 600m in less than 7m traveled), leads from the Highveld of the Haenertsburg area to the Lowveld adjoining the Kruger National Park. The town is famous for its flowering cherries, azaleas and the Cherry Blossom Festival in spring.


Summary:
The town was named after Carl Ferdinand Haenert who came to South Africa from Germany in 1857 and made the first gold discoveries here. Dating back to the gold rush the village has retained its old-world atmosphere with shops built in the style of old corrugated mining houses. Trading posts with names like “Never Despair” and “New Found Out” sell collectables and memorabilia and the bookstore “Memory-Hold-The-Door” you will find a wide selection of books on the Anglo-Boer war and the Makgoba War (a war that lasted from 1888 to 1895 about the resistance of Chief Makgoba and his BaTlou tribe against the annexation of their land).

Haenertsburg has the second largest indigenous forest in the country in the larger Magoebaskloof area. For an breathtaking experience of the Letaba River Gorge in Magoebaskloof zipline over the forest canopy will give you a bird's-eye-view of the giant waterfall, wild flowers and a variety of bird species.

There are 18 avian species on the Red Data list in the Haenertsburg area. The Black-fronted Bush-shrike, Black Rumped Buttonquail and the Blue Swallow are resident in the Woodbush Forest Reserve where our guide, David Letsoalo will introduce us to the birdlife and take us to the tallest planted tree in Africa. David started off as a potter in Polokwane who became interested in identifying different birds that flew into the studio. He was fascinated by the variety he saw and with the help of the Robertson bible on birds, and bird courses he was able to ditch his day job and became bird guide. David has been birding for 23 years and is a regular bird guide for tourists and has even been interviewed by BBC he says proudly.

For home-grown coffee, head for Krabbefontein Coffee farm - the highest coffee plantation in the country. Here coffee farmer Zander Ernst will take us up the hill where the coffee trees grow in the shade of the forest, protected from frost and wind. The smell of raw plucked coffee beans being harvested has a unique smell that is different from the rich aromatic scent of roasted beans.

What is a place without its art? We meet Alicia Boshoff, film fabricator and fashion designer from Mystic Creations. “Whatever you can dream of, I can make it,” says Alicia. She has worked on numerous film sets creating props, wardrobe and unique wearable art pieces for award winning movies like Mad Max. She moved from the city to a farm in Haenertsburg a few years ago where she draws her inspiration from nature and wild animals like eagles and owls to create her tribal infused designs using leather, feathers and crystals.

There is something mystic about Magoebaskloof that nurtures creatives and gives them freedom of expression. Or maybe it's all that fresh air and mountain water, but whatever it is, this little village is truly magic.

FINAL Script: Haenertsburg
Duration: 10.42 minutes
Date: 9 July 2025

VO1 There’s a little village on the slopes of the Wolkberg mountains near Tzaneen in Limpopo………. It’s called Haenertsburg…… population: 500.

PAUSE

It’s a town with a rich history….,but we’re enticed by the forest on its outskirts…….. We’ve heard it’s home to characters as fascinating as Haenertsburg itself.

PAUSE

VO2 In keeping with the theme of the trip, it’s a journey that starts unexpectedly: a zipline through the forest canopy

LINK: Let’s go! And I just hold this one, and then I just lean back and then slide…Let’s go!
Woow! Woow!

UPS waterfalls

VO3 The Letaba River flows through the area splitting into smaller rivers along the way…..

UPS small river

At daybreak the mist rises over the valley. They call this place Land of the Silver mist.

PAUSE

Alicia Boshoff: I find, when I look outside my studio, as you can see, like you can see eagles flying and you see this beautiful mountain. It’s so inspiring. I love to work with nature.

UPs dog

Masa Kekana: Alicia, tell me what inspires you?

Alicia Boshoff: What inspires me? I think everything. I think nature, a lot of fantasy. I think Game of Thrones, Lord of the Rings. This is all part of my life growing up.

VO4 Artist Alicia Boshoff moved from the city to Magoebaskloof a few years ago. She’s arguably the area’s most famous resident, but she spends much of her time alone, creating a fantasy world.

Alicia Boshoff: Costume designer: So I love that I get to create my own world. It’s almost when you go on a movie job they say make the craziest post-apocalyptic world possible and then you get to do the masks. And that excites me a lot. Waking up in the morning, let’s make a headdress for Madusa.

Masa Kekana: (laughs):

Alicia Boshoff: (laughs) You know what I mean?

Masa Kekana: You must have a crazy wild imagination?

Alicia Boshoff: 10;21;03 I really do. (Laughs)

VO5 Alicia is an award-winning designer of post-apocolyptic costumes. She worked on Mad Max - the Hollywood blockbuster starring our own Charlize Theron - which won an Oscar for Best Costume Design.

Alicia Boshoff: I had a team of 10 people and at the end of the day we will have this little bits of leather and little bits of cloth, things lying on the floor and for the next day we would like ok this is what we are going to use as masks. Because we had to think in a way that if it is the apocalypse. People are going to be in rubbish dumps looking for plastics looking for little bits of things and that’s what they are going to use..

Masa Kekana: Scraps here and there

Alicia Boshoff: Yah, basically to construct their garments.

UPSOUND NATURAL WALKING INTO STUDIO
UPS: Masa Kekana: Shu Alicia, you have quite the imagination. Tell me about some of these costumes you designed.

Alicia Boshoff: So these were actually some of the masks for Mad Max. And this was also from another character where this is a Death Character.

Masa Kekana: Ooh one is supposed to be dark hey?

Alicia Boshoff: Yeah she was painted black, she had a skull on her head. This is also the head dress all made out of leaves.

Masa Kekana: Oh I see. I see your inspiration of nature in your work in the small detail ... .these leaves as well. Oh that’s a veil.

Alicia Boshoff: Yah. That’s her face. She’s quite a creepy character.

Masa Kekana: Yah. Mission accomplished.

UPs laughter

Visual seque

UPsound Ziplining through forest

VO6 Magoebaskloof was named after King Mamphoku Makgoba, a Chief of the Sotho tribe, who ruled in the late 1800’s and means Makgoba’s ravine… Back then it was prized land…. and still is.

UPsound - pouring a cup of coffee

VO7 These fertile and frost free mountains are ideal for coffee - drinking and harvesting. Krabbefontein in Magoebaskloof is the highest commercial coffee farm in the country.

Upsound: Zander Ernts: We focus on high altitude farming, so all our coffee is planted 1100 meters and higher….

Short pause

Masa Kekana: Zander, this space that you have brought us to is…it’s peaceful, it’s beautiful.

Zander Ernst: Coffee farmer: It’s beautiful in the sense that these mountains are actually warm mountains. We don’t have the frost that the Drakensberg has. Climatically it is amazing.

VO8 Zander Ernst is a first generation coffee farmer. Here on the slopes of the Wolkberg mountain small pockets of coffee grow in the shade of tall trees, protecting them from wind and direct sun.

Masa Kekana: Your journey I believe began when you rescued a coffee tree? First of all how do you rescue a coffee tree?

Zander Ernst: In my garden I actually found a coffee tree by chances. I initially thought it was a Mahogany and then later on saw a cherry. It’s the first time I saw a cherry on a tree.

Masa Kekana: I would really like you to show me the coffee bean because from here it looks like a berry from here. I can’t imagine coffee beans in there.

Zander Ernts: You know you split open the cherry like this. So I think….first thing, obviously coffee is a cherry.

Masa Kekana: Wait, coffee is a cherry?

Zander Ernst: Yah.

Masa Kekana: Wow. I did not expect to find this in here.

UPS - Ziplining: Masa: Ooh!! Woow. Wow! Incredible.

UPs Music

VO9 The significance of trees in this area extends beyond their commercial value. Back in the forest I meet a man whose connection with them is almost spiritual.

UPs David Letsoalo walking through forest with a bit of Music

VO10 David Letsoalo knows the forest like the back of his hand, and along with trees is fascinated by birds.

David Letsoalo: I like outdoors, and when I started working as a pottery assistant is when my employer asked me to identify the birds which were coming to the feeder. And that sparked everything.

VO11 His interest in birds was sparked a quarter of a century ago..

David Letsoalo: She decided to buy me a bird book as a Christmas present. That’s where it all started

Masa Kekana: And are there things that are specific to this forest that you won’t find in any other forest?

David Letsoalo: Bird guide: In this forest we’ve got the bird called the black fronted bush shrike. So you get him only in this forest. We’ve lost some of the species which used to occur around here. The granite grassland before the plantation of pine and eucalyptus they use to boost things like Blue Swallows, all those species are gone.
Oh! The bird calling behind us is the Grey Cuckoo-Shrike. It's a high pitch call. Shhh… He stopped calling but it is a high pitch call. He’s got… he’s just flown across.

Masa Kekana: I love the way you talk about the birds, like they are your cousins.

David Letsoalo: Laughs

Masa Kekana: You talk about them like they are your cousins.

David Letsoalo: (Laughs). I enjoy birding, I enjoy watching them and listening.

Masa Kekana: You've made me enjoy listening too…..laughter

VO12 It’s astonishing to behold. David knows the sound of every bird call in this area, known as the Woodbush Forest Reserve.

David Letsoalo: Forrest birding can be very difficult. We rely a lot on calls and feeding party. You can walk for about 2 hours without hearing a bird then all of a sudden all of the birds are there.

UPS David Letsoalo: As you can see…it is all these tall trees. So there is one that is marked.

UPs Masa Kekakan: Wow! Here it is.

David Letsoalo: The tallest planted tree in the world.

VO13 Woodbush is the second largest forest in the country, and home to record-breaking trees.

David Letsoalo: Where we are now, we are at the tallest planted trees, which were planted between 1905, 1906.

UPs birds

VO14 The giant Sydney Blue gum was planted over a century ago. It’s close to 88 meters tall and is still growing.
Pause
It was planted at a defining moment in our country: the aftermath of the second Anglo-Boer war and the rush that followed the discovery of gold here in the late 1800’s. More than a hundred years later and it is still standing.

LINK: It really is quite a sensory experience being in this forest. From everything we see to things that you smell, things that you touch and of course what you hear. It’s magical.

VO15 We came here expecting to tell the story of a small town with an undoubtedly textured history. But we were drawn to people who might still consider Haenertsburg their home but surely believe the forest is where their heart is.

UPS Music over sunset
end

VO She’s an award-winning designer creating post-apocalyptic costumes from a place deep in the forest.

Because we had to think in a way that if it is the apocalypse. People are going to be in rubbish dumps looking for plastics looking for little bits of things and that’s what they are going to use.. Masa Kekana: Scraps here and there Alicia Boshoff: Yah, basically to construct their garments. UPSOUND NATURAL WALKING INTO STUDIO UPS: Masa Kekana: Shu Alicia, you have quite the imagination. Tell me about some of these costumes you designed. Alicia Boshoff: So these were actually some of the masks for Mad Max. And this was also from another character where this is a Death Character. Masa Kekana: Ooh one is supposed to be dark hey? Alicia Boshoff: Yeah she was painted black, she had a skull on her head. This is also the head dress all made out of leaves. Masa Kekana: Oh I see. I see your inspiration of nature in your work in the small detail ... .these leaves as well. Oh that’s a veil. Alicia Boshoff: Yah. That’s her face. She’s quite a creepy character. Masa Kekana: Yah. Mission accomplished. UPs laughter Visual seque UPsound Ziplining through forest VO6 Magoebaskloof was named after King Mamphoku Makgoba, a Chief of the Sotho tribe, who ruled in the late 1800’s and means Makgoba’s ravine… Back then it was prized land…. and still is. UPsound - pouring a cup of coffee VO7 These fertile and frost free mountains are ideal for coffee - drinking and harvesting. Krabbefontein in Magoebaskloof is the highest commercial coffee farm in the country. Upsound: Zander Ernts: We focus on high altitude farming, so all our coffee is planted 1100 meters and higher…. Short pause Masa Kekana: Zander, this space that you have brought us to is…it’s peaceful, it’s beautiful. Zander Ernst: Coffee farmer: It’s beautiful in the sense that these mountains are actually warm mountains. We don’t have the frost that the Drakensberg has. Climatically it is amazing. VO8 Zander Ernst is a first generation coffee farmer. Here on the slopes of the Wolkberg mountain small pockets of coffee grow in the shade of tall trees, protecting them from wind and direct sun. Masa Kekana: Your journey I believe began when you rescued a coffee tree? First of all how do you rescue a coffee tree? Zander Ernst: In my garden I actually found a coffee tree by chances. I initially thought it was a Mahogany and then later on saw a cherry. It’s the first time I saw a cherry on a tree. Masa Kekana: I would really like you to show me the coffee bean because from here it looks like a berry from here. I can’t imagine coffee beans in there. Zander Ernts: You know you split open the cherry like this. So I think….first thing, obviously coffee is a cherry. Masa Kekana: Wait, coffee is a cherry? Zander Ernst: Yah. Masa Kekana: Wow. I did not expect to find this in here. UPS - Ziplining: Masa: Ooh!! Woow. Wow! Incredible. UPs Music VO9 The significance of trees in this area extends beyond their commercial value. Back in the forest I meet a man whose connection with them is almost spiritual. UPs David Letsoalo walking through forest with a bit of Music VO10 David Letsoalo knows the forest like the back of his hand, and along with trees is fascinated by birds. David Letsoalo: I like outdoors, and when I started working as a pottery assistant is when my employer asked me to identify the birds which were coming to the feeder. And that sparked everything. VO11 His interest in birds was sparked a quarter of a century ago.. David Letsoalo: She decided to buy me a bird book as a Christmas present. That’s where it all started Masa Kekana: And are there things that are specific to this forest that you won’t find in any other forest? David Letsoalo: Bird guide: In this forest we’ve got the bird called the black fronted bush shrike. So you get him only in this forest. We’ve lost some of the species which used to occur around here. The granite grassland before the plantation of pine and eucalyptus they use to boost things like Blue Swallows, all those species are gone. Oh! The bird calling behind us is the Grey Cuckoo-Shrike. It's a high pitch call. Shhh… He stopped calling but it is a high pitch call. He’s got… he’s just flown across. Masa Kekana: I love the way you talk about the birds, like they are your cousins. David Letsoalo: Laughs Masa Kekana: You talk about them like they are your cousins. David Letsoalo: (Laughs). I enjoy birding, I enjoy watching them and listening. Masa Kekana: You've made me enjoy listening too…..laughter VO12 It’s astonishing to behold. David knows the sound of every bird call in this area, known as the Woodbush Forest Reserve. David Letsoalo: Forrest birding can be very difficult. We rely a lot on calls and feeding party. You can walk for about 2 hours without hearing a bird then all of a sudden all of the birds are there. UPS David Letsoalo: As you can see…it is all these tall trees. So there is one that is marked. UPs Masa Kekakan: Wow! Here it is. David Letsoalo: The tallest planted tree in the world. VO13 Woodbush is the second largest forest in the country, and home to record-breaking trees. David Letsoalo: Where we are now, we are at the tallest planted trees, which were planted between 1905, 1906. UPs birds VO14 The giant Sydney Blue gum was planted over a century ago. It’s close to 88 meters tall and is still growing. Pause It was planted at a defining moment in our country: the aftermath of the second Anglo-Boer war and the rush that followed the discovery of gold here in the late 1800’s. More than a hundred years later and it is still standing. LINK: It really is quite a sensory experience being in this forest. From everything we see to things that you smell, things that you touch and of course what you hear. It’s magical. VO15 We came here expecting to tell the story of a small town with an undoubtedly textured history. But we were drawn to people who might still consider Haenertsburg their home but surely believe the forest is where their heart is. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): From the highest coffee farm in the land, to rare birds and the tallest tree in the world, Haenertsburg in Magoebaskloof is a village shrouded in mist and a history dating back to the gold rush.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Haenertsburg is a little village on the slopes of the Wolkberg mountains in Magoebaskloof near Tzaneen in Limpopo. Rising 1,550 meters above sea level, the town is often shrouded in mist and clouds giving it the apt name of “Land of the Silver Mist”. The steepest mountain pass in South Africa, the Magoebaskloof pass (falling approximately 600m in less than 7m traveled), leads from the Highveld of the Haenertsburg area to the Lowveld adjoining the Kruger National Park. The town is famous for its flowering cherries, azaleas and the Cherry Blossom Festival in spring.
metadata.Summary: The town was named after Carl Ferdinand Haenert who came to South Africa from Germany in 1857 and made the first gold discoveries here. Dating back to the gold rush the village has retained its old-world atmosphere with shops built in the style of old corrugated mining houses. Trading posts with names like “Never Despair” and “New Found Out” sell collectables and memorabilia and the bookstore “Memory-Hold-The-Door” you will find a wide selection of books on the Anglo-Boer war and the Makgoba War (a war that lasted from 1888 to 1895 about the resistance of Chief Makgoba and his BaTlou tribe against the annexation of their land). Haenertsburg has the second largest indigenous forest in the country in the larger Magoebaskloof area. For an breathtaking experience of the Letaba River Gorge in Magoebaskloof zipline over the forest canopy will give you a bird's-eye-view of the giant waterfall, wild flowers and a variety of bird species. There are 18 avian species on the Red Data list in the Haenertsburg area. The Black-fronted Bush-shrike, Black Rumped Buttonquail and the Blue Swallow are resident in the Woodbush Forest Reserve where our guide, David Letsoalo will introduce us to the birdlife and take us to the tallest planted tree in Africa. David started off as a potter in Polokwane who became interested in identifying different birds that flew into the studio. He was fascinated by the variety he saw and with the help of the Robertson bible on birds, and bird courses he was able to ditch his day job and became bird guide. David has been birding for 23 years and is a regular bird guide for tourists and has even been interviewed by BBC he says proudly. For home-grown coffee, head for Krabbefontein Coffee farm - the highest coffee plantation in the country. Here coffee farmer Zander Ernst will take us up the hill where the coffee trees grow in the shade of the forest, protected from frost and wind. The smell of raw plucked coffee beans being harvested has a unique smell that is different from the rich aromatic scent of roasted beans. What is a place without its art? We meet Alicia Boshoff, film fabricator and fashion designer from Mystic Creations. “Whatever you can dream of, I can make it,” says Alicia. She has worked on numerous film sets creating props, wardrobe and unique wearable art pieces for award winning movies like Mad Max. She moved from the city to a farm in Haenertsburg a few years ago where she draws her inspiration from nature and wild animals like eagles and owls to create her tribal infused designs using leather, feathers and crystals. There is something mystic about Magoebaskloof that nurtures creatives and gives them freedom of expression. Or maybe it's all that fresh air and mountain water, but whatever it is, this little village is truly magic. __________________________________________________________________________________________________
